newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Conflicting food aid claims in Sri Lanka war zone.
newsitem.headline: Conflicting food aid claims in Sri Lanka war zone.

text.p: A U.N. official on Thursday dismissed claims that the Sri Lankan Government was using food as a weapon in its 13-year-old war against rebels fighting for a separate Tamil state.

"I know no other case in the world where a government is committed to feeding everyone in a war zone where its stated enemy is operational," said Joseph Scalise, country director of the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP).
"Food is not being used as a weapon in this war," Scalise said, adding that WFP monitoring of the food situation in the north of the Indian Ocean island thus far showed no "humanitarian catastrophe."
The official's comments, in an interview with Reuters, came as overseas Tamil activists launched an "awareness week" to highlight Tamil suffering in northern and eastern Sri Lanka.

"The international community is not fully aware of the extent of the atrocities perpetrated on the Tamil people in the north and east of Sri Lanka," the International Federation of Tamils said in a statement.

"Aid given by the international community for Tamils in the north and east is prevented by the Sri Lankan government from reaching them," the federation said. "The government is using food as weapon to subjugate the Tamils."
But Scalise said claims by separatist Tamil rebels of massive starvation in conflict areas were "grossly inaccurate".
The government was sending more than 7,000 tonnes of food each month to the north, enough to feed approximately half a million people, he said.
This was in addition to food assistance given by international aid agencies like the WFP, he added.
Frances Stevenson, coordinator for the French aid agency Medecins Sans Frontieres, said she saw undernutrition but no malnutrition or starvation.
"Unlike malnutrition, (undernutrition) has no serious effect on their health," she said. A greater concern, she added, was that "all basic essential drugs are in short supply".

Separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels have blamed the government and international aid agencies for ignoring hundreds of thousands of Tamils displaced by the army's recent offensives to capture northern rebel-held territory.
Tight government bans on journalists' travel to the affected areas makes it impossible to independently verify the claims.
Tamil civilians moving from rebel-held areas to the government-held frontline town of Vavuniya told Reuters food was in short supply but said they saw no signs of starvation.
Rice production in the northern Kilinochchi district suffered due to a severe drought earlier this year and all food items to the area now had to come from Colombo, they said.

The LTTE is fighting a war for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east. Nearly 74 percent of Sri Lanka's 18 million people are Sinhalese, while around 13 percent are Tamils, who say they suffer discrimination.

Almost 600,000 Tamils have been displaced since last October, when Sri Lankan forces launched an offensive to capture the LTTE's stronghold in the northern Jaffna peninsula, according to government figures.
The Sri Lankan government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the conflict, while the LTTE says a much higher number have perished.
